segments_english.text: This technique is the GP twin of the AP's symmetric selection, and it turns product problems into one-line algebra.
The picture on the board says it all: place terms as a over r, a, and a r, and when you multiply, the r in the denominator cancels the r on top, leaving a clean a cubed.
So for three terms in GP, always take a over r, a, a r. Their product is simply a cubed, and one unknown disappears immediately.
For five terms, extend outward with the same idea: a over r squared, a over r, a, a r, a r squared, multiplying to a to the fifth.

<curious> Now the even case, which hides a twist worth memorising. For four terms use a over r cubed, a over r, a r, a r cubed — and notice the ratio between these symmetric terms is r squared, not r.
The payoff mirrors the AP exactly: a two-unknown product problem collapses to a single unknown the moment you switch to symmetric terms.
<whisper> And that even-count ratio is precisely where students stumble — the spacing there is r squared, the perfect analogue of the AP's two-d trap. Never carry a bare r into the even case.

segments_hinglish.text: यह technique AP की symmetric selection की GP twin है, और यह product problems को one-line algebra में बदल देती है।
board पर picture सब कह देती है: terms को a over r, a, और a r रखो, और जब तुम multiply करते हो, denominator का r ऊपर के r को cancel कर देता है, बचता है clean a cubed।
तो GP में तीन terms के लिए, हमेशा a over r, a, a r लो। इनका product बस a cubed है, और एक unknown तुरंत गायब हो जाता है।
पाँच terms के लिए, वही idea बाहर बढ़ाओ: a over r squared, a over r, a, a r, a r squared, जिनका product a to the fifth है।
<curious> अब even case, जो memorise करने लायक एक twist छुपाए है। चार terms के लिए use करो a over r cubed, a over r, a r, a r cubed — और ध्यान दो इन symmetric terms के बीच ratio r squared है, r नहीं।
payoff AP को बिलकुल mirror करता है: दो-unknown वाला product problem symmetric terms पर switch करते ही एक unknown में सिमट जाता है।
<whisper> और वही even-count ratio है जहाँ students लड़खड़ाते हैं — वहाँ spacing r squared है, AP के two-d trap का perfect analogue। even case में कभी bare r मत ले जाओ।

29.title: Three numbers in GP from product and pairwise sum

board_content.text: Product of 3 GP terms is 216; sum of pairwise products is 156. Find them.
Take the terms symmetrically as $\tfrac{a}{r}, a, a r$.
$r = 3$ or $r = \tfrac13$ give the SAME set, just reversed.
Answer: the numbers are 2, 6, 18.

segments_english.text: Let's open the GP examples with a board classic that rewards symmetric selection. The product of three GP terms is two hundred sixteen, and the sum of their pairwise products is one hundred fifty-six.
Immediately take the terms symmetrically as a over r, a, and a r — this is exactly what the technique is for.
The product is clean: a over r times a times a r is a cubed, and setting that to two hundred sixteen gives a equals six. One unknown gone.
For the pairwise products, factoring out a squared leaves a squared times one over r plus r plus one equals one hundred fifty-six, which reduces to one over r plus r equals ten thirds.
Multiply through and you get three r squared minus ten r plus three equals zero, which factors neatly as three r minus one times r minus three.
<curious> So r is either three or one third — but notice these give the very same set of numbers, just listed in reverse order.
Either way, the three numbers are two, six, and eighteen. Symmetric selection turned a two-unknown tangle into one clean quadratic.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो GP examples एक board classic से खोलें जो symmetric selection का इनाम देता है। तीन GP terms का product two hundred sixteen है, और उनके pairwise products का sum one hundred fifty-six।
तुरंत terms को symmetrically a over r, a, और a r लो — technique इसी के लिए है।
product clean है: a over r times a times a r है a cubed, और इसे two hundred sixteen रखने पर a equals six मिलता है। एक unknown गया।
pairwise products के लिए, a squared बाहर निकालने पर बचता है a squared times one over r plus r plus one equals one hundred fifty-six, जो घटकर one over r plus r equals ten thirds बनता है।
इसे multiply करो और मिलता है three r squared minus ten r plus three equals zero, जो साफ़ factor होता है three r minus one times r minus three।
<curious> तो r या तो three है या one third — पर ध्यान दो ये same set of numbers देते हैं, बस उल्टे order में listed।
किसी भी तरह, तीन numbers हैं two, six, और eighteen। symmetric selection ने दो-unknown वाली उलझन को एक clean quadratic में बदल दिया।

30.title: A recurring decimal is a convergent GP

board_content.text: Express 0.3̄ = 0.3333… as a fraction
Write it as an infinite GP of place-value pieces.
The convergence check $|r| = \tfrac{1}{10} < 1$ is what LICENSES the formula.
Every recurring decimal is secretly a convergent GP.

segments_english.text: This example reveals a hidden GP inside something totally familiar — a repeating decimal. We want to write nought point three recurring as an exact fraction.
The trick is to break the decimal into its place-value pieces, which turns out to be an infinite geometric series.
Written out, it is three tenths plus three hundredths plus three thousandths, and so on forever — each piece one tenth of the one before.
So the first term is three tenths and the ratio is one tenth. Crucially, the size of that ratio is well below one, so the infinite sum exists.
Apply the sum-to-infinity formula: three tenths over nine tenths, which simplifies to exactly one third.
<whisper> Notice what earned us the right to use the formula — the convergence check. The ratio is one tenth, comfortably under one, and only that check licenses the whole calculation.
The takeaway is worth carrying: every recurring decimal is secretly a convergent GP, so you can always convert one to a fraction this way.

segments_hinglish.text: यह example एक बिलकुल familiar चीज़ के अंदर छुपी GP दिखाता है — एक repeating decimal। हम nought point three recurring को एक exact fraction लिखना चाहते हैं।
trick है decimal को उसके place-value pieces में तोड़ना, जो निकलता है एक infinite geometric series।
लिखने पर, यह है three tenths plus three hundredths plus three thousandths, और ऐसे ही हमेशा — हर piece पिछले का one tenth।
तो first term है three tenths और ratio है one tenth। crucially, उस ratio की size one से काफ़ी नीचे है, तो infinite sum exist करता है।
sum-to-infinity formula apply करो: three tenths over nine tenths, जो घटकर exactly one third बनता है।
<whisper> ध्यान दो किसने हमें formula use करने का हक़ दिया — convergence check। ratio one tenth है, आराम से one के नीचे, और सिर्फ़ वही check पूरे calculation को license करता है।
यह takeaway साथ ले जाने लायक है: हर recurring decimal चुपके से एक convergent GP है, तो तुम हमेशा इसे इस तरह fraction में बदल सकते हो।

board_content.text: Infinite GP has sum 2 and its cubes sum to 24. Find a and r.
The cubes form a GP with ratio $r^3$.
$(2r+1)(r+2)=0$: $|r|<1$ rejects $r = -2$, leaving $r = -\tfrac12$.
So $r = -\tfrac12$ and $a = 3$; check: $27 / (9/8) = 24\;\checkmark$.

segments_english.text: Here two infinite sums pin down a GP, and the convergence condition does the final selecting. The sum of the GP is two, and the sum of the cubes of its terms is twenty-four.
From the first fact, a over one minus r equals two, so a equals two times one minus r. That is our first relation.
Now the cubes. Cubing every term produces a new GP whose ratio is r cubed, so its sum is a cubed over one minus r cubed.
Setting that equal to twenty-four and substituting a cubed equals eight times one minus r cubed, the eights and a factor of one minus r cancel down nicely.

After simplifying with the difference-of-cubes factorisation, you land on one minus r squared over one plus r plus r squared equals three, which rearranges to two r squared plus five r plus two equals zero.
<whisper> That factors as two r plus one times r plus two, giving r equals minus one half or minus two. But the convergence condition rejects minus two outright, since its size exceeds one.
So the ratio is minus one half and the first term is three. A quick check confirms it: twenty-seven over nine eighths is indeed twenty-four.

segments_hinglish.text: यहाँ दो infinite sums एक GP को pin करते हैं, और convergence condition final selection करती है। GP का sum two है, और उसके terms के cubes का sum twenty-four।
पहले fact से, a over one minus r equals two, तो a equals two times one minus r। यही हमारा पहला relation है।
अब cubes। हर term को cube करने पर एक नई GP बनती है जिसका ratio r cubed है, तो उसका sum है a cubed over one minus r cubed।
इसे twenty-four के बराबर रखकर और a cubed equals eight times one minus r cubed substitute करके, eights और एक one minus r factor अच्छे से cancel हो जाते हैं।

difference-of-cubes factorisation से simplify करने पर, तुम one minus r squared over one plus r plus r squared equals three पर पहुँचते हो, जो rearrange होकर two r squared plus five r plus two equals zero बनता है।

<whisper> यह factor होता है two r plus one times r plus two, देता है r equals minus one half या minus two। पर convergence condition minus two को सीधे reject करती है, क्योंकि उसकी size one से ज़्यादा है।
तो ratio है minus one half और first term three। एक quick check इसे confirm करता है: twenty-seven over nine eighths सच में twenty-four है।

board_content.text: First two GP terms sum to 12; third and fourth sum to 48; terms alternate in sign.

board_content.latex: a + a r = 12, \qquad a r^2 + a r^3 = 48

board_content.text: Divide the second equation by the first.
'Alternately positive and negative' forces $r < 0$, so $r = -2$.
Answer: first term $a = -4$.

segments_english.text: This AIEEE problem shows how a single qualitative phrase can decide everything. The first two terms add to twelve, the third and fourth add to forty-eight, and we are told the terms alternate in sign.
Write both facts algebraically: a plus a r equals twelve, and a r squared plus a r cubed equals forty-eight.
The clean move is to divide the second equation by the first — the common factor of one plus r will cancel.
After cancelling, a r squared times one plus r over a times one plus r reduces to r squared, and the right side is forty-eight over twelve, so r squared equals four, meaning r is plus or minus two.
<whisper> Here the words do the work. Alternately positive and negative forces the ratio to be negative, so we discard plus two and keep minus two.
Now substitute back. With r equals minus two, a times one plus r is a times minus one, which equals twelve, so a is minus four.
So the first term is minus four. That one qualitative phrase — alternating signs — was the entire constraint that picked minus two over plus two.

segments_hinglish.text: यह AIEEE problem दिखाता है कि एक अकेला qualitative phrase कैसे सब कुछ decide कर सकता है। पहले दो terms twelve में add होते हैं, तीसरा और चौथा forty-eight में, और बताया गया है कि terms sign में alternate करते हैं।
दोनों facts algebraically लिखो: a plus a r equals twelve, और a r squared plus a r cubed equals forty-eight।
clean move है दूसरी equation को पहली से divide करना — one plus r का common factor cancel हो जाएगा।
cancel करने के बाद, a r squared times one plus r over a times one plus r घटकर r squared बनता है, और right side है forty-eight over twelve, तो r squared equals four, यानी r plus या minus two है।
<whisper> यहाँ शब्द काम करते हैं। alternately positive and negative ratio को negative होने पर मजबूर करता है, तो हम plus two हटाकर minus two रखते हैं।
अब वापस substitute करो। r equals minus two के साथ, a times one plus r है a times minus one, जो twelve के बराबर है, तो a है minus four।
तो first term है minus four। वो एक qualitative phrase — alternating signs — पूरा constraint था जिसने plus two के बजाय minus two चुना।

board_content.text: Joining midpoints halves the area each time.
Infinite nesting, yet a finite total — the signature payoff of $|r| < 1$.

segments_english.text: Here is the geometry problem that makes convergence tangible. Start with a square of side sixteen centimetres, join the midpoints to make a second square inside, then repeat forever.
The board shows the nesting. The key geometric fact is that joining the midpoints of a square produces a new square with exactly half the area.
So the areas form a shrinking sequence, and we recognise it as a GP the moment we compute the first area.
The outer square has area sixteen squared, which is two hundred fifty-six square centimetres — that is our first term.
Each later area is half the one before, giving two hundred fifty-six, one hundred twenty-eight, sixty-four, and so on. So the ratio is one half, comfortably below one.
The total area is then two hundred fifty-six over one minus one half, which comes to five hundred twelve square centimetres.
<excited> Sit with how strange and beautiful that is — you nest squares infinitely many times, yet the areas add up to a perfectly finite number. That is the signature payoff of a convergent GP.

segments_hinglish.text: यह रहा वो geometry problem जो convergence को tangible बना देता है। sixteen centimetres side के square से शुरू करो, midpoints जोड़कर अंदर दूसरा square बनाओ, फिर हमेशा दोहराओ।
board nesting दिखा रहा है। key geometric fact यह है कि एक square के midpoints जोड़ने से exactly आधी area वाला नया square बनता है।
तो areas एक shrinking sequence बनाती हैं, और पहली area compute करते ही हम इसे GP पहचान लेते हैं।
outer square की area है sixteen squared, यानी two hundred fifty-six square centimetres — यही हमारा first term है।
हर बाद की area पिछले की आधी है, देती है two hundred fifty-six, one hundred twenty-eight, sixty-four, और ऐसे ही। तो ratio है one half, आराम से one के नीचे।
total area तब है two hundred fifty-six over one minus one half, जो five hundred twelve square centimetres आता है।

<excited> इसके साथ बैठो कि यह कितना अजीब और खूबसूरत है — तुम squares को infinitely many times nest करते हो, फिर भी areas एक बिलकुल finite number में जुड़ती हैं। यही convergent GP का signature payoff है।

board_content.text: For positive a, b, c prove $(a+b+c)\left(\tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1c\right) \ge 9$
Apply AM ≥ GM to each triple separately.
Multiplying two AM–GMs is one of the highest-yield Advanced moves.
Equality holds iff $a = b = c$.

segments_english.text: This is a signature Advanced technique — proving an inequality by multiplying two applications of AM ≥ GM. We must show the product of a-plus-b-plus-c and its reciprocal sum is at least nine.
The plan is to hit each factor with the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality on its own.
For the first factor, a plus b plus c is at least three times the cube root of the product a b c.
For the second factor, one over a plus one over b plus one over c is at least three times the cube root of one over a b c — the same inequality applied to the reciprocals.
<curious> Now multiply the two inequalities, both of whose sides are positive. The cube root of a b c and its reciprocal cancel completely, leaving nine on the right.
So the whole product is at least nine, exactly as required. This multiply-two-AM-GMs move appears again and again in Advanced problems.
And the equality tells you the extreme case: everything is tight precisely when a, b, and c are all equal.

segments_hinglish.text: यह एक signature Advanced technique है — AM ≥ GM के दो applications को multiply करके inequality prove करना। हमें दिखाना है कि a-plus-b-plus-c और उसके reciprocal sum का product कम से कम nine है।
plan यह है कि हर factor पर अलग से arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality लगाई जाए।
पहले factor के लिए, a plus b plus c कम से कम three times the cube root of the product a b c है।
दूसरे factor के लिए, one over a plus one over b plus one over c कम से कम three times the cube root of one over a b c है — वही inequality reciprocals पर लगाई गई।
<curious> अब दोनों inequalities को multiply करो, जिनके दोनों sides positive हैं। a b c का cube root और उसका reciprocal पूरी तरह cancel हो जाते हैं, right पर nine बचता है।
तो पूरा product कम से कम nine है, बिलकुल जैसा चाहिए था। यह multiply-two-AM-GMs move Advanced problems में बार-बार आता है।
और equality तुम्हें extreme case बताती है: सब कुछ tight exactly तब होता है जब a, b, और c सब बराबर हों।

35.title: Each term equals the sum of the next two

board_content.text: In a GP of positive terms, each term = sum of the next two. Find r.
Write the condition on a single representative term.

board_content.latex: a = a r + a r^2 \;\Rightarrow\; 1 = r + r^2

board_content.text: Positive terms reject the negative root, leaving $r = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$.
This is the reciprocal of the golden ratio.

segments_english.text: This AIEEE problem has a wonderfully clean setup: in a GP of positive terms, each term equals the sum of the next two. We want the common ratio.
Because every term obeys the same rule, we can write the condition on just one representative term and its two successors.
That gives a equals a r plus a r squared. Dividing through by a, since a is nonzero, leaves one equals r plus r squared.
Rearranged, this is the quadratic r squared plus r minus one equals zero — short, but loaded.
The quadratic formula gives r equals minus one plus or minus root five, all over two.
<whisper> Now the positivity of the terms decides between the roots. The negative root would make terms negative, so we reject it and keep root five minus one over two.
And there is a lovely surprise in the answer: this value is exactly the reciprocal of the golden ratio, the number that shows up throughout nature and art.

segments_hinglish.text: इस AIEEE problem का setup बेहद clean है: positive terms की एक GP में, हर term अगले दो का sum है। हमें common ratio चाहिए।
चूँकि हर term same rule मानता है, हम condition को सिर्फ़ एक representative term और उसके दो successors पर लिख सकते हैं।
इससे मिलता है a equals a r plus a r squared। a से divide करने पर, चूँकि a nonzero है, बचता है one equals r plus r squared।
rearrange करने पर, यह है quadratic r squared plus r minus one equals zero — छोटी, पर loaded।
quadratic formula देता है r equals minus one plus or minus root five, over two।
<whisper> अब terms की positivity roots के बीच decide करती है। negative root terms को negative बना देता, तो हम इसे reject करके root five minus one over two रखते हैं।
और answer में एक प्यारी surprise है: यह value exactly golden ratio का reciprocal है, वो number जो nature और art में हर जगह दिखता है।

36.title: The chessboard grains, in closed form

board_content.text: 1 grain on square 1, doubling to square 64. Total grains?
The counts form a GP: $a = 1$, $r = 2$, $n = 64$.
A concrete demonstration of why $r > 1$ growth 'detonates'.
More grains than all the wheat ever grown on Earth.

segments_english.text: We close the GP examples by returning to the chessboard legend and computing it exactly. One grain on the first square, doubling each square, all the way to the sixty-fourth.
The grain counts form a textbook GP — first term one, ratio two, and sixty-four terms in all.
Written out, the counts are one, two, four, and so on up to two to the sixty-third on the final square.
Apply the sum formula: a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one, which is one times two to the sixty-fourth minus one, all over two minus one.
Since the denominator is just one, the total is two to the sixty-fourth minus one — roughly one point eight times ten to the nineteenth grains.
<excited> That is a staggering number, and it makes the abstract point vivid: growth with a ratio above one truly detonates by the end, no matter how gently it starts.
To put it in perspective, that is more grains of wheat than have ever been grown in all of human history.

grain counts एक textbook GP बनाते हैं — first term one, ratio two, और कुल sixty-four terms।
लिखने पर, counts हैं one, two, four, और ऐसे ही final square पर two to the sixty-third तक।
sum formula apply करो: a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one, यानी one times two to the sixty-fourth minus one, over two minus one।
चूँकि denominator बस one है, total है two to the sixty-fourth minus one — लगभग one point eight times ten to the nineteenth grains।
<excited> यह एक staggering number है, और यह abstract point को vivid बना देता है: one से ऊपर ratio वाली growth अंत तक सच में detonate करती है, चाहे शुरुआत कितनी भी gentle हो।
perspective में रखें तो, यह पूरे मानव इतिहास में उगाए गए सारे गेहूँ के दानों से भी ज़्यादा है।

37.title: GP: the trap list and the pro-tips

board_content.text: GP — the traps that cost marks, and the shortcuts that save them
Convergence: never write $S_\infty = \tfrac{a}{1-r}$ without checking $|r| < 1$.
Sign of $r$: don't drop the $r < 0$ alternating case.
GM sign: $b = \pm\sqrt{ac}$; a GP cannot contain a zero term.
Even symmetric pick uses ratio $r^2$; and $r = 1$ means $S_n = na$, not division.
Pro-tip: given a PRODUCT, use $\tfrac{a}{r}, a, a r$; for '$a,b,c$ in GP' use $b^2 = ac$.
Take logs to convert a GP problem into the (often easier) AP toolkit.
Every recurring decimal is a convergent GP — recognise it on sight.

segments_english.text: Let's gather the GP traps that quietly cost marks, and the shortcuts that win them back.
The number-one GP error, and the chapter's most punished slip, is writing the sum-to-infinity formula without first checking that the size of r is below one. Make that check a reflex.
Second, respect the sign of r. Dropping the negative-ratio, alternating-sign case loses whole problems, and picking the wrong sign when two roots survive is a classic slip.
Third, the geometric mean is plus or minus the root of a c — choose the sign that keeps a real GP. And never accept a solution that forces a term to zero, because a GP can never contain a zero.
Two more: the even symmetric selection uses ratio r squared, not r, and when r equals one the sum is simply n times a — do not blindly divide by r minus one.

<curious> Now the winning reflexes. Given a product, switch to a over r, a, a r to collapse the unknowns; and for any three-in-GP condition, reach straight for b squared equals a c rather than introducing a and r.
Keep the log bridge handy too — taking logs turns a GP problem into an AP problem, and the AP toolkit is often the easier one to swing.
And carry this recognition into the exam hall: every recurring decimal is a convergent GP in disguise, so you can always convert one to a fraction the instant you spot it.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो GP traps इकट्ठा करें जो चुपके से marks खाते हैं, और वो shortcuts जो उन्हें वापस जिताते हैं।
number-one GP error, और chapter का सबसे ज़्यादा punish होने वाला slip, है sum-to-infinity formula लिखना बिना पहले check किए कि r की size one से नीचे है। उस check को reflex बना लो।
दूसरा, r के sign का सम्मान करो। negative-ratio, alternating-sign case छोड़ देना पूरे problems गँवा देता है, और जब दो roots बचें तो गलत sign चुनना एक classic slip है।
तीसरा, geometric mean है plus या minus root of a c — वो sign चुनो जो एक real GP रखे। और ऐसा कोई solution कभी मत मानो जो किसी term को zero पर मजबूर करे, क्योंकि GP में कभी zero नहीं हो सकता।
दो और: even symmetric selection ratio r squared use करती है, r नहीं, और जब r equals one हो तो sum बस n times a है — आँख मूँदकर r minus one से divide मत करो।

<curious> अब winning reflexes। product दिया हो, तो a over r, a, a r पर switch करके unknowns collapse करो; और किसी भी three-in-GP condition के लिए, a और r introduce करने के बजाय सीधे b squared equals a c reach करो।
log bridge भी पास रखो — logs लेने से GP problem एक AP problem बन जाता है, और AP toolkit अक्सर घुमाने में आसान होता है।
और यह recognition exam hall में ले जाओ: हर recurring decimal disguise में एक convergent GP है, तो जैसे ही spot करो, उसे तुरंत fraction में बदल सकते हो।

39.title: The HM formula and the p-q reciprocal trick

board_content.text: Two results that flow from reciprocating
If $a, H, b$ are in HP, then $\tfrac1a, \tfrac1H, \tfrac1b$ are in AP.
For 'pth term $=q$, qth term $=p$', work in the reciprocal AP.
The reciprocate-first habit turns messy HP algebra into one line of AP work.

segments_english.text: Let's derive the two HP results you'll lean on, and both fall straight out of reciprocating.
Take three numbers a, H, b in harmonic progression. By definition their reciprocals — one over a, one over H, one over b — are in arithmetic progression.
So one over H is just the arithmetic mean of one over a and one over b, which tidies to a plus b over two a b.
Flip that over and you have the harmonic mean of two numbers: H equals two a b over a plus b. Notice the two in the numerator — that is where students most often slip.
The second result is the famous set-up where the p-th term is q and the q-th term is p. The move is to work entirely in the reciprocal AP, never the HP itself.
Subtracting the two reciprocal-AP equations gives p minus q times d equals one over q minus one over p, which is p minus q over p q — so the common difference d is one over p q.
<curious> Back-substituting, the n-th reciprocal is n over p q, so the n-th HP term is p q over n. In particular, the p-plus-q-th term is p q over p plus q — a beautifully clean result.
The lesson beneath both derivations is one habit: reciprocate first. It turns messy HP algebra into a single line of routine AP work.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो दो HP results derive करें, और दोनों reciprocating से सीधे निकलते हैं।
तीन numbers a, H, b को harmonic progression में लो। definition से इनके reciprocals — one over a, one over H, one over b — arithmetic progression में हैं।
तो one over H बस one over a और one over b का arithmetic mean है, जो साफ़ होकर a plus b over two a b बनता है।
इसे flip करो और तुम्हें दो numbers का harmonic mean मिल जाता है: H equals two a b over a plus b। numerator में two पर ध्यान दो — यहीं students सबसे ज़्यादा फिसलते हैं।
दूसरा result वो famous set-up है जहाँ p-th term q है और q-th term p। move यह है कि पूरा काम reciprocal AP में करो, कभी HP में नहीं।
दोनों reciprocal-AP equations को subtract करने पर मिलता है p minus q times d equals one over q minus one over p, यानी p minus q over p q — तो common difference d है one over p q।
<curious> वापस substitute करने पर, n-th reciprocal है n over p q, तो n-th HP term है p q over n। ख़ासकर, p-plus-q-th term है p q over p plus q — एक बेहद clean result।
दोनों derivations के नीचे एक ही habit है: reciprocate first। यह messy HP algebra को routine AP काम की एक line में बदल देती है।

board_content.text: Definition, nth term, means — all via the reciprocal AP

board_content.latex: a_n \text{ in HP} \iff \frac{1}{a_n} \text{ in AP} \;\;(\text{no zero terms})

board_content.text: HM uses $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ — the '2' is essential; and there is NO sum formula.

segments_english.text: Let's consolidate the HP toolkit. Every formula here is really an AP formula seen through the reciprocal.
The definition anchors it all: a sequence is in HP exactly when the reciprocals of its terms are in AP — and, crucially, no term may be zero, since you cannot reciprocate zero.
The n-th term is one over the quantity one over a plus n minus one times d, where d is the common difference of that reciprocal AP.
For two numbers, the harmonic mean is two a b over a plus b — the single most-used HP formula.
For a whole list, the harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of the reciprocals — the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals.
To insert n harmonic means, insert n arithmetic means between the reciprocals of a and b, so one over H-k equals one over a plus k times D, with D the reciprocal-AP step.
And the bridge to the next unit: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, with the means ordered A at least G at least H.
<whisper> Two warnings to carry. The harmonic mean has a two on top — forget it and you get a wrong answer that looks plausible. And there is no sum formula for an HP; never invent one.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो HP toolkit consolidate करें। यहाँ हर formula असल में reciprocal से देखा गया एक AP formula है।
definition सबको anchor करती है: एक sequence HP में तभी है जब उसके terms के reciprocals AP में हों — और crucially, कोई term zero नहीं हो सकता, क्योंकि zero को reciprocate नहीं कर सकते।
n-th term है one over the quantity one over a plus n minus one times d, जहाँ d उस reciprocal AP का common difference है।
दो numbers के लिए, harmonic mean है two a b over a plus b — सबसे ज़्यादा use होने वाला HP formula।
पूरी list के लिए, harmonic mean है n divided by reciprocals का sum — reciprocals के average का reciprocal।
n harmonic means insert करने के लिए, a और b के reciprocals के बीच n arithmetic means insert करो, तो one over H-k equals one over a plus k times D, जिसमें D reciprocal-AP step है।
और अगले unit का bridge: arithmetic mean times harmonic mean equals geometric mean squared, means के order A कम से कम G कम से कम H के साथ।
<whisper> दो warnings साथ ले जाओ। harmonic mean के ऊपर एक two है — इसे भूलो और तुम्हें एक गलत answer मिलता है जो plausible दिखता है। और HP के लिए कोई sum formula नहीं है; इसे कभी मत बनाओ।

41.title: HM of 4 and 12, and verifying AH = G²

board_content.text: Find the HM of 4 and 12, and verify $AH = G^2$
Now compute the arithmetic and geometric means too.
The identity $AH = G^2$ holds exactly — a fast self-check on any means problem.

segments_english.text: Let's start the HP examples with a clean computation that also verifies the key identity. We want the harmonic mean of four and twelve.
Apply the formula directly: two times four times twelve over four plus twelve, which is ninety-six over sixteen, giving six.
Now, to test the identity, let's also find the other two means of the same pair.
The arithmetic mean is four plus twelve over two, which is eight. The geometric mean is the square root of forty-eight, or four root three.
The identity claims the product of the arithmetic and harmonic means equals the geometric mean squared. So check the left side: eight times six is forty-eight.
And the right side: four root three, squared, is also forty-eight. The two match perfectly.
<curious> So the identity holds exactly, and that is worth keeping as a lightning self-check — any time you compute A, G, and H, confirm that A times H equals G squared.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो HP examples एक clean computation से शुरू करें जो key identity भी verify करता है। हमें four और twelve का harmonic mean चाहिए।
formula सीधे apply करो: two times four times twelve over four plus twelve, यानी ninety-six over sixteen, जो six देता है।
अब, identity test करने के लिए, चलो उसी pair के बाकी दो means भी निकालें।
arithmetic mean है four plus twelve over two, यानी eight। geometric mean है square root of forty-eight, या four root three।
identity कहती है कि arithmetic और harmonic means का product geometric mean squared के बराबर है। तो left side check करो: eight times six है forty-eight।
और right side: four root three, squared, भी forty-eight है। दोनों perfectly match करते हैं।
<curious> तो identity exactly hold करती है, और इसे एक lightning self-check की तरह रखना worth है — जब भी तुम A, G, और H compute करो, confirm करो कि A times H equals G squared।

42.title: Finding the 10th term from two given terms

board_content.text: 3rd term of an HP is ⅐, 7th term is 1⁄15. Find the 10th term.
Reciprocate: the reciprocals form an AP.
Flip back at the very end: the 10th HP term is $\tfrac{1}{21}$.
Answer: the 10th term is 1⁄21.

segments_english.text: This example is the reciprocate-first habit in pure form. We are given the third term of an HP as one seventh and the seventh term as one fifteenth.
The move is automatic: flip everything over, because the reciprocals of an HP form an arithmetic progression that we can attack directly.
So in the reciprocal AP, the third term is seven and the seventh term is fifteen.
The common difference is the change in value over the change in position: fifteen minus seven over seven minus three, which is eight over four, equal to two.
Now find the first reciprocal term: seven minus two times two is three. Then the tenth reciprocal is three plus nine times two, which is twenty-one.
<whisper> Here is the step students forget — flip back. We were working with reciprocals, so the tenth HP term is one over twenty-one, not twenty-one itself.
So the tenth term of the harmonic progression is one over twenty-one.

segments_hinglish.text: यह example reciprocate-first habit का pure रूप है। हमें एक HP का third term one seventh और seventh term one fifteenth दिया गया है।
move automatic है: सब कुछ flip करो, क्योंकि एक HP के reciprocals एक arithmetic progression बनाते हैं जिस पर हम सीधे हमला कर सकते हैं।
तो reciprocal AP में, third term है seven और seventh term है fifteen।
common difference है value के change over position के change: fifteen minus seven over seven minus three, यानी eight over four, बराबर two।
अब first reciprocal term निकालो: seven minus two times two है three। फिर tenth reciprocal है three plus nine times two, यानी twenty-one।
<whisper> यह रहा वो step जो students भूल जाते हैं — flip back। हम reciprocals के साथ काम कर रहे थे, तो tenth HP term है one over twenty-one, twenty-one खुद नहीं।
तो harmonic progression का tenth term है one over twenty-one।

43.title: The p-th term is q, the q-th term is p

board_content.text: pth term of an HP is q, qth term is p. Find the (p+q)th and nth terms.
Reciprocate to an AP with first term $A_0$, common difference $d$.
A result worth memorising outright — it recurs across JEE Main.

segments_english.text: This is a JEE Main staple, and the reciprocate-first habit makes it almost trivial. The p-th term of an HP is q, and the q-th term is p.
As always, drop into the reciprocal AP. Call its first term A-nought and its common difference d.
The two facts become two clean AP equations: A-nought plus p minus one times d is one over q, and A-nought plus q minus one times d is one over p.
Subtract them and the d falls out beautifully — you find the common difference is one over p q, and the same value drops out for the first term A-nought.
So the n-th reciprocal is one over p q plus n minus one times one over p q, which collapses neatly to n over p q.
<curious> Flipping back, the n-th HP term is p q over n. And so the p-plus-q-th term is simply p q over p plus q — the whole messy problem in one line of AP algebra.
This answer is worth memorising outright. The p-th-equals-q, q-th-equals-p pattern recurs across JEE Main, and the clean formula a-n equals p q over n saves real time.

segments_hinglish.text: यह JEE Main का staple है, और reciprocate-first habit इसे लगभग trivial बना देती है। एक HP का p-th term q है, और q-th term p।
हमेशा की तरह, reciprocal AP में उतरो। इसका first term A-nought और common difference d कहो।
दोनों facts दो clean AP equations बन जाते हैं: A-nought plus p minus one times d है one over q, और A-nought plus q minus one times d है one over p।
इन्हें subtract करो और d खूबसूरती से निकल जाता है — तुम पाते हो common difference one over p q है, और वही value first term A-nought के लिए भी निकलती है।
तो n-th reciprocal है one over p q plus n minus one times one over p q, जो साफ़ होकर n over p q बनता है।
<curious> flip back करने पर, n-th HP term है p q over n। और इसलिए p-plus-q-th term बस p q over p plus q है — पूरा messy problem AP algebra की एक line में।
यह answer सीधे memorise करने लायक है। p-th-equals-q, q-th-equals-p pattern JEE Main में बार-बार आता है, और clean formula a-n equals p q over n असली time बचाता है।

board_content.text: Insert 4 harmonic means between 1 and 1⁄6
Insert 4 AMs between the reciprocals $\tfrac11 = 1$ and $\tfrac{1}{1/6} = 6$.
The HMs are the reciprocals of the interior AP terms.
Always work the means in the reciprocal AP, then flip back.

segments_english.text: Inserting harmonic means is pure reciprocate-first. We must place four harmonic means between one and one sixth.
So we swing over to the reciprocal AP and instead insert four arithmetic means between the reciprocals — one over one, which is one, and one over one sixth, which is six.
The common difference of that reciprocal AP is six minus one over four plus one, which is exactly one — very clean.
So the reciprocal AP reads one, two, three, four, five, six, with the four inserted means sitting neatly in the middle.
Now flip back: the harmonic means we actually want are the reciprocals of those interior AP terms.
<curious> That gives one half, one third, one quarter, and one fifth — a satisfyingly tidy set of harmonic means.
The whole technique is the same every time: do all the mean-inserting in the reciprocal AP, then reciprocate the interior terms back at the end.

तो हम reciprocal AP की तरफ़ मुड़ते हैं और इसके बजाय reciprocals के बीच चार arithmetic means insert करते हैं — one over one, यानी one, और one over one sixth, यानी six।

45.title: Recovering numbers from AM and HM

board_content.text: The AM of two numbers is 9 and their HM is 4. Find the numbers.
Use $AH = G^2$ to get the geometric mean first.
The means triad pins the numbers without ever solving the HM equation directly.

segments_english.text: This example shows the three means working together as a team. We are told the arithmetic mean of two numbers is nine and their harmonic mean is four.
The clever first step is to route through the identity. The geometric mean squared equals the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean.
So G squared is nine times four, which is thirty-six, meaning the geometric mean is six. We now have all three means without touching the messy harmonic-mean equation.
The two means we care about give us a sum and a product: a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean, eighteen, and a times b is the geometric mean squared, thirty-six.
A sum and a product mean the numbers are roots of a quadratic: x squared minus eighteen x plus thirty-six equals zero.
Solving, x equals nine plus or minus the root of eighty-one minus thirty-six, which is nine plus or minus three root five.
<excited> Notice the elegance — the triad of means pinned the two numbers down without our ever having to solve the awkward harmonic-mean equation directly.

clever पहला step है identity के रास्ते जाना। geometric mean squared equals arithmetic mean times harmonic mean।
तो G squared है nine times four, यानी thirty-six, मतलब geometric mean six है। अब हमारे पास तीनों means हैं, बिना messy harmonic-mean equation को छुए।
जो दो means हमें चाहिए वो एक sum और एक product देते हैं: a plus b है twice the arithmetic mean, eighteen, और a times b है geometric mean squared, thirty-six।
एक sum और एक product का मतलब numbers एक quadratic के roots हैं: x squared minus eighteen x plus thirty-six equals zero।
solve करने पर, x equals nine plus or minus root of eighty-one minus thirty-six, यानी nine plus or minus three root five।
<excited> elegance पर ध्यान दो — means की triad ने दोनों numbers को pin कर दिया, बिना हमें awkward harmonic-mean equation सीधे solve किए।

board_content.text: If a, b, c are in HP, prove a/(b+c), b/(c+a), c/(a+b) are in HP
Start from the definition: reciprocals are in AP.
Multiply through by the constant $(a+b+c)$ — still an AP.
Reciprocate that AP ⇒ $\tfrac{a}{b+c}, \tfrac{b}{c+a}, \tfrac{c}{a+b}$ are in HP. ∎

segments_english.text: We finish the HP examples with a proof that showcases the signature reciprocate-and-manipulate chain. We must show that if a, b, c are in HP, then a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b are also in HP.
Begin from the definition. Because a, b, c are in HP, their reciprocals — one over a, one over b, one over c — are in AP.
Now the manipulation. Multiplying an AP by a nonzero constant keeps it an AP, so multiply through by a plus b plus c.
That gives a plus b plus c over a, over b, and over c — still an arithmetic progression.
Next, subtract one from each term. Subtracting the same constant from every term of an AP leaves an AP, and each term becomes b plus c over a, c plus a over b, a plus b over c.

<curious> Now reciprocate that AP one final time. The reciprocals of an AP form an HP, and those reciprocals are exactly a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b — which is what we wanted to prove.
That reciprocate-and-manipulate sequence is the signature HP proof technique: flip to an AP, scale and shift freely, then flip back.

segments_hinglish.text: हम HP examples को एक proof से खत्म करते हैं जो signature reciprocate-and-manipulate chain दिखाता है। हमें दिखाना है कि अगर a, b, c HP में हैं, तो a over b plus c, b over c plus a, और c over a plus b भी HP में हैं।
definition से शुरू करो। चूँकि a, b, c HP में हैं, उनके reciprocals — one over a, one over b, one over c — AP में हैं।
अब manipulation। एक AP को nonzero constant से multiply करना उसे AP ही रखता है, तो a plus b plus c से multiply करो।
इससे मिलता है a plus b plus c over a, over b, और over c — अभी भी एक arithmetic progression।
अगला, हर term से one घटाओ। AP के हर term से same constant घटाना AP ही छोड़ता है, और हर term बन जाता है b plus c over a, c plus a over b, a plus b over c।
<curious> अब उस AP को एक आखिरी बार reciprocate करो। एक AP के reciprocals एक HP बनाते हैं, और वो reciprocals exactly a over b plus c, b over c plus a, और c over a plus b हैं — जो हमें prove करना था।
वो reciprocate-and-manipulate sequence signature HP proof technique है: AP में flip करो, आज़ादी से scale और shift करो, फिर flip back।

47.title: HP: the trap list and the pro-tips

board_content.text: HP — the traps that cost marks, and the shortcuts that save them
Signature trap: attacking HP terms directly instead of reciprocating.
Missing '2': writing $\tfrac{ab}{a+b}$ instead of $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ for the HM.
Never invent a sum formula for an HP — there is none in general.
No zero terms allowed; reversing $A \ge G \ge H$ is a shared trap with Unit 5.
Pro-tip: reciprocate first, use the AP toolkit, flip back at the end.
For 'pth $=q$, qth $=p$', the answer is $a_n = \tfrac{pq}{n}$ — memorise it.
Remember HM ≤ GM ≤ AM: the HM is always the smallest, pulled toward the smaller number.

segments_english.text: Let's gather the HP traps that quietly cost marks, then the shortcuts that win them back.
The signature HP error is attacking the terms directly instead of reciprocating. If you find yourself grinding on the HP terms themselves, stop and flip.
The second trap is dropping the two: writing a b over a plus b for the harmonic mean instead of two a b over a plus b. That missing factor of two is a silent, plausible-looking mistake.
Third, never invent a closed-form sum for an HP. There genuinely isn't one, so if a question needs the sum, telescope it or sum termwise — we'll see that in Unit eight.
Two more: no term of an HP may be zero, and reversing the mean chain — writing H at least G at least A — is a trap shared with the next unit.
<curious> Now the winning reflex, and it is the whole subtopic: reciprocate first, run the full AP toolkit, and flip back only at the very end.
And memorise the p-q result outright — when the p-th term is q and the q-th is p, the n-th term is p q over n. It appears often enough to be worth instant recall.
Finally, keep the ordering in muscle memory: harmonic is at most geometric is at most arithmetic. The harmonic mean is always the smallest, pulled toward the smaller of the two numbers.

48.title: Three means for three different questions

AM = $\tfrac{a+b}{2}$ — the average when quantities ADD.
GM = $\sqrt{ab}$ — the average when quantities MULTIPLY (growth, CAGR).
HM = $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ — the average of RATES over a fixed task.

segments_english.text: This unit ties the three classical means together. The key realisation is that there is more than one honest way to average two positive numbers, and each mean answers a different question.
The arithmetic mean, a plus b over two, is the right average when quantities add — marks, costs, distances.
The geometric mean, root a b, is the right average when quantities multiply. The average yearly return that turns one rupee into the same final corpus is the geometric mean, never the arithmetic one.
The harmonic mean, two a b over a plus b, is the right average of rates over a fixed task — the round-trip speed we met in the last unit.

The board shows the deep result: for two distinct positive numbers, these three always sit in the same order between a and b, with the harmonic nearest the smaller, the arithmetic nearest the larger, and the geometric in between.
<curious> So the ordering is fixed and strict: arithmetic above geometric above harmonic, collapsing to a single point only when the two numbers are equal.
And they are locked together by one identity: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared — which means the three means themselves form a geometric progression.
There is a lovely consequence hiding in that identity: the geometric mean is simultaneously the GM of the original pair and the GM of the arithmetic-and-harmonic pair.

arithmetic mean, a plus b over two, सही average है जब quantities add करती हैं — marks, costs, distances।
geometric mean, root a b, सही average है जब quantities multiply करती हैं। वो average yearly return जो एक rupee को same final corpus में बदलता है, geometric mean है, कभी arithmetic नहीं।
harmonic mean, two a b over a plus b, fixed task पर rates का सही average है — वही round-trip speed जो हम पिछले unit में मिले।
board deep result दिखा रहा है: दो distinct positive numbers के लिए, ये तीनों हमेशा a और b के बीच same order में बैठते हैं, harmonic छोटे के पास, arithmetic बड़े के पास, और geometric बीच में।
<curious> तो ordering fixed और strict है: arithmetic ऊपर geometric ऊपर harmonic, एक single point पर सिमटता है सिर्फ़ तब जब दोनों numbers बराबर हों।
और वे एक identity से आपस में locked हैं: arithmetic mean times harmonic mean equals geometric mean squared — जिसका मतलब है तीनों means खुद एक geometric progression बनाते हैं।
उस identity में एक प्यारा consequence छुपा है: geometric mean एक साथ original pair का GM है और arithmetic-and-harmonic pair का भी GM।

49.title: Proving the chain and recovering the numbers

board_content.text: Four short proofs that hold the unit together
So $\tfrac{A}{G} = \tfrac{G}{H}$: the means form a GP.
Recover the numbers: $a + b = 2A$ and $ab = G^2$, so by Vieta:

board_content.latex: x^2 - 2Ax + G^2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; a, b = A \pm \sqrt{A^2 - G^2}

board_content.text: Real (and positive) iff $A \ge G$ — the discriminant IS the mean inequality.

segments_english.text: Four short proofs hold this whole unit together, and none takes more than a line or two.

Start with the central identity. The arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean is a plus b over two, times two a b over a plus b — the a plus b factors cancel, leaving a b, which is the geometric mean squared.
Rearranged, that says A over G equals G over H, so the three means are in geometric progression with G as their middle term.

For the inequality, use the fact we planted earlier: the square of root a minus root b is never negative. Expand it and you immediately get a plus b over two is at least root a b — the arithmetic mean beats the geometric.

Now chain to the harmonic. Since H equals G squared over A, and A is at least G, dividing gives G squared over A at most G squared over G, which is G. So G is at least H, completing the chain A at least G at least H.
The fourth result recovers the original numbers from their means. We know a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean and a times b is the geometric mean squared.
By Vieta's formulas the numbers are roots of x squared minus two A x plus G squared, giving a and b equal to A plus or minus the root of A squared minus G squared.
<whisper> And here is the elegant twist. Those roots are real and positive exactly when A is at least G — so the discriminant condition is nothing other than the mean inequality itself.

segments_hinglish.text: चार short proofs इस पूरे unit को जोड़े रखते हैं, और कोई भी एक-दो line से ज़्यादा नहीं लेता।
central identity से शुरू करो। arithmetic mean times harmonic mean है a plus b over two, times two a b over a plus b — a plus b factors cancel हो जाते हैं, बचता है a b, जो geometric mean squared है।
rearrange करने पर, यह कहता है A over G equals G over H, तो तीनों means geometric progression में हैं, G उनके middle term के रूप में।

inequality के लिए, वो fact use करो जो हमने पहले बोया था: root a minus root b का square कभी negative नहीं। इसे expand करो और तुम्हें तुरंत मिलता है a plus b over two कम से कम root a b — arithmetic mean geometric को हरा देता है।

अब harmonic तक chain करो। चूँकि H equals G squared over A, और A कम से कम G है, divide करने पर G squared over A ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा G squared over G, यानी G। तो G कम से कम H है, chain A कम से कम G कम से कम H पूरी।
चौथा result original numbers को उनके means से recover करता है। हम जानते हैं a plus b twice the arithmetic mean है और a times b geometric mean squared।
Vieta के formulas से numbers हैं x squared minus two A x plus G squared के roots, देते हैं a और b बराबर A plus or minus root of A squared minus G squared।
<whisper> और यह रहा elegant twist। वो roots real और positive exactly तब हैं जब A कम से कम G हो — तो discriminant condition mean inequality के अलावा और कुछ नहीं है।

50.title: The means, the identity, and the recovery quadratic

board_content.text: Everything for two positive reals a, b

board_content.latex: AH = G^2 \iff A, G, H \text{ in GP}
A \ge G \ge H, \quad \text{equality iff } a = b

board_content.text: Reality condition: real numbers exist iff $A \ge G$. If $A < G$, none do.
For $n$ numbers: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, equality iff all are equal.

segments_english.text: Let's consolidate the compact formula set for two positive reals. Keep these together — they interlock.
The three means: arithmetic is a plus b over two, geometric is root a b, and harmonic is two a b over a plus b.
The core identity binds them: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, which is the same as saying the three means form a geometric progression.
The ordering is fixed: arithmetic is at least geometric is at least harmonic, with equality throughout only when the two numbers are equal.
To recover the numbers from their means, centre a quadratic on the arithmetic mean: x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero.
Its roots are a and b equal to the arithmetic mean plus or minus the root of the arithmetic mean squared minus the geometric mean squared.
<whisper> And carry the reality condition: real numbers exist exactly when the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean. If a problem hands you A below G, no such real pair exists.
Finally, everything generalises to n numbers: arithmetic mean is at least geometric mean is at least harmonic mean, with equality only when all the numbers are equal.

तीनों means: arithmetic है a plus b over two, geometric है root a b, और harmonic है two a b over a plus b।
core identity इन्हें बाँधती है: arithmetic mean times harmonic mean equals geometric mean squared, जो यही कहने जैसा है कि तीनों means एक geometric progression बनाते हैं।
ordering fixed है: arithmetic कम से कम geometric कम से कम harmonic, equality पूरी तरह सिर्फ़ तब जब दोनों numbers बराबर हों।
means से numbers recover करने के लिए, एक quadratic को arithmetic mean पर centre करो: x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero।
इसके roots हैं a और b बराबर arithmetic mean plus or minus root of arithmetic mean squared minus geometric mean squared।
<whisper> और reality condition ले जाओ: real numbers exactly तब exist करते हैं जब arithmetic mean कम से कम geometric mean हो। अगर कोई problem तुम्हें A, G से नीचे दे, तो ऐसा कोई real pair मौजूद नहीं।
आखिर में, सब कुछ n numbers तक generalise होता है: arithmetic mean कम से कम geometric mean कम से कम harmonic mean, equality सिर्फ़ तब जब सारे numbers बराबर हों।

51.title: Recovering the numbers from AM and GM

board_content.text: The AM of two positive numbers is 10 and their GM is 8. Find them.
Equivalently $a, b = 10 \pm \sqrt{100 - 64} = 10 \pm 6$.
$A = 10 > G = 8$, so real roots exist — the check is automatic.
Answer: the numbers are 4 and 16.

segments_english.text: This is the signature board question for the unit — recovering two numbers from their arithmetic and geometric means. Here the arithmetic mean is ten and the geometric mean is eight.
Translate the means into a sum and a product. The sum a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean, so twenty; the product a b is the geometric mean squared, so sixty-four.
A sum and a product mean the two numbers are roots of a quadratic: x squared minus twenty x plus sixty-four equals zero.
This factors cleanly as x minus four times x minus sixteen, so the numbers are four and sixteen.
You can also read them straight off the recovery formula: ten plus or minus the root of one hundred minus sixty-four, which is ten plus or minus six.
<curious> And notice the reality check took care of itself — the arithmetic mean, ten, is comfortably larger than the geometric mean, eight, so real roots were guaranteed from the start.
So the two numbers are four and sixteen.

segments_hinglish.text: यह unit का signature board question है — दो numbers को उनके arithmetic और geometric means से recover करना। यहाँ arithmetic mean ten है और geometric mean eight।
means को एक sum और एक product में translate करो। sum a plus b है twice the arithmetic mean, तो twenty; product a b है geometric mean squared, तो sixty-four।
एक sum और एक product का मतलब दोनों numbers एक quadratic के roots हैं: x squared minus twenty x plus sixty-four equals zero।
यह साफ़ factor होता है x minus four times x minus sixteen, तो numbers हैं four और sixteen।
तुम इन्हें recovery formula से सीधे भी पढ़ सकते हो: ten plus or minus root of one hundred minus sixty-four, यानी ten plus or minus six।
<curious> और ध्यान दो reality check खुद ही संभल गया — arithmetic mean, ten, geometric mean, eight, से आराम से बड़ा है, तो real roots शुरू से guaranteed थे।
तो दोनों numbers हैं four और sixteen।

53.title: Ordering the means and spotting the GP

board_content.text: For two distinct positive numbers, order A, G, H and name the GP
Distinct positives ⇒ the inequality is strict.
From $AH = G^2$, the triple $A, G, H$ is a GP.
So $A, G, H$ is a DECREASING GP whose middle term (GM) is $G$.
That $G$ is the very same GM of the original two numbers.

segments_english.text: This example locks in both the ordering and the hidden progression among the means, for two distinct positive numbers.
Because the numbers are distinct, the mean inequality is strict — no ties are possible.
So the ordering is a clean, strict chain: the arithmetic mean is greater than the geometric, which is greater than the harmonic.
Now the structure. From the identity that A times H equals G squared, the three means themselves form a geometric progression.
Its common ratio is G over A, which also equals H over G, and since A is the largest, that ratio is below one.
<curious> So the means form a decreasing geometric progression, and its middle term — the geometric mean of A and H — is exactly G.
And here is the satisfying closure: that G in the middle is the very same geometric mean of the original two numbers we started with. The whole picture folds together neatly.

segments_hinglish.text: यह example दो distinct positive numbers के लिए means के बीच ordering और छुपी progression दोनों को lock करता है।
चूँकि numbers distinct हैं, mean inequality strict है — कोई ties संभव नहीं।
तो ordering एक clean, strict chain है: arithmetic mean geometric से बड़ा है, जो harmonic से बड़ा है।
अब structure। उस identity से कि A times H equals G squared, तीनों means खुद एक geometric progression बनाते हैं।
इसका common ratio है G over A, जो H over G के भी बराबर है, और चूँकि A सबसे बड़ा है, वो ratio one से नीचे है।
<curious> तो means एक decreasing geometric progression बनाते हैं, और इसका middle term — A और H का geometric mean — exactly G है।
और यह रहा संतोषजनक closure: वो बीच वाला G उन्हीं दो original numbers का geometric mean है जिनसे हमने शुरू किया था। पूरी picture करीने से एक साथ मुड़ जाती है।

54.title: The numbers and their ratio from A and G

board_content.text: Two positives have AM = A and GM = G. Express them and find their ratio.
This comes straight from the recovery quadratic.
The ratio depends only on $A/G$, not on $A$ and $G$ separately.
The numbers are real iff $A \ge G$ — the same reality condition again.
A common Advanced form writes $A : G = (m+n) : 2\sqrt{mn}$.

segments_english.text: This Advanced example generalises the recovery, expressing the two numbers and their ratio purely in terms of their arithmetic and geometric means.
The numbers come straight from the recovery quadratic: a and b equal the arithmetic mean plus or minus the root of the arithmetic mean squared minus the geometric mean squared.
There is nothing new to derive here — it is exactly the roots of x squared minus two A x plus G squared, read off directly.
Their ratio is then the larger root over the smaller: A plus the root of A squared minus G squared, all over A minus that same root.

<curious> And here is the structural insight. If you divide top and bottom by A, the ratio depends only on the single quantity A over G — not on A and G separately. The shape of the pair is set entirely by how far apart the two means are.
Keep the reality condition in view: the numbers are real exactly when the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean — the same discriminant condition once more.
A common Advanced form writes the ratio of A to G as m plus n to two root m n, which is just this same relationship dressed in a substitution.

numbers recovery quadratic से सीधे आते हैं: a और b बराबर arithmetic mean plus or minus root of arithmetic mean squared minus geometric mean squared।
यहाँ derive करने को कुछ नया नहीं — यह exactly x squared minus two A x plus G squared के roots हैं, सीधे पढ़े गए।
इनका ratio तब है larger root over smaller: A plus root of A squared minus G squared, over A minus वही root।

<curious> और यह रहा structural insight। अगर तुम ऊपर-नीचे को A से divide करो, ratio सिर्फ़ एक quantity A over G पर depend करता है — A और G पर अलग-अलग नहीं। pair का shape पूरी तरह इस बात से तय होता है कि दोनों means कितने दूर हैं।
reality condition नज़र में रखो: numbers real exactly तब हैं जब arithmetic mean कम से कम geometric mean हो — वही discriminant condition एक बार फिर।
एक common Advanced form A to G के ratio को m plus n to two root m n लिखता है, जो बस यही relationship एक substitution में सजा हुआ है।

55.title: AM/GM/HM: the traps and the pro-tips

board_content.text: Means relationship — the traps, and the fast moves
Direction trap: writing the chain backwards as $H \ge G \ge A$.
Reality: $A \ge G$ is exactly the real-roots condition for the board quadratic.
Centre the recovery quadratic on $A$, not on $G$.
Pro-tip: to find two numbers from means, jump to $x^2 - 2Ax + G^2 = 0$.
For min/max of $x + \tfrac{k}{x}$-type expressions, AM ≥ GM gives it in one line.
Equality $a = b$ always locates the optimiser.
Sanity check: $G$ is the middle term of the GP $A, G, H$ — a fast ordering test.

segments_english.text: Let's close with the traps and the fast moves for the means relationship.
The single most common error is writing the chain backwards — harmonic at least geometric at least arithmetic. Fix the true direction in memory: arithmetic is the biggest.

Second, connect the reality condition to quadratics: A at least G is exactly the condition for the recovery quadratic to have real roots, because the discriminant is four times A squared minus G squared.
Third, centre that recovery quadratic on the arithmetic mean, not the geometric. The coefficient of x is minus two A, and the constant is G squared — mixing these up is a classic slip.
<curious> Now the pro-tips. To find two numbers from their means, jump straight to x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero — no need to reconstruct anything.
For minimum or maximum of x-plus-k-over-x type expressions, the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality gives the answer in a single line, far faster than calculus.
And the equality case always locates the optimiser: the extreme is reached exactly when the two quantities are equal.
Finally, a fast sanity check on any ordering: the geometric mean must be the middle term of the geometric progression A, G, H. If it is not sitting in the middle, you have the order wrong.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो means relationship के traps और fast moves के साथ बंद करें।
सबसे common error है chain को उल्टा लिखना — harmonic कम से कम geometric कम से कम arithmetic। सही direction memory में fix करो: arithmetic सबसे बड़ा है।
दूसरा, reality condition को quadratics से जोड़ो: A कम से कम G exactly वो condition है जिससे recovery quadratic के real roots हों, क्योंकि discriminant four times A squared minus G squared है।
तीसरा, उस recovery quadratic को arithmetic mean पर centre करो, geometric पर नहीं। x का coefficient minus two A है, और constant G squared — इन्हें मिला देना एक classic slip है।
<curious> अब pro-tips। दो numbers को उनके means से निकालने के लिए, सीधे x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero पर कूदो — कुछ भी reconstruct करने की ज़रूरत नहीं।
x-plus-k-over-x type expressions के minimum या maximum के लिए, arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality एक ही line में answer देती है, calculus से कहीं fast।
और equality case हमेशा optimiser locate करती है: extreme exactly तब पहुँचता है जब दोनों quantities बराबर हों।
आखिर में, किसी भी ordering का fast sanity check: geometric mean को geometric progression A, G, H का middle term होना चाहिए। अगर यह बीच में नहीं बैठा, तो तुम्हारा order गलत है।

board_content.caption: AP part times GP part, term by term, makes the AGP

board_content.text: Present-value sums in finance are exactly AGP sums.
Neither the AP nor the GP sum formula works alone — but the GP trick does.
Multiply the whole sum by $r$, shift by one, subtract: the AP collapses to $d$.
When $|r| < 1$, the AGP converges: geometric decay beats linear growth.
Recognise an AGP by its shape: (linear in $n$) × ($r^{\,n-1}$).

segments_english.text: Now a progression that fuses the two we already know. Think of an arithmetico-geometric progression as a GP whose terms are being steadily re-weighted by a growing counter.
The board makes it concrete. Take an AP on top, a GP below, and multiply them term by term — the geometric decay of r to the k multiplied by the linear march of the AP.
So the general term is a plus n minus one times d, all times r to the n minus one — the AP factor and the GP factor multiplied together.
This is not just an abstraction. Present-value and expected-value calculations in finance — steadily growing payments each discounted by a fixed factor — are exactly AGP sums.
Here is the defining challenge for summation: because each term carries both an additive and a multiplicative pattern, neither the AP sum formula nor the GP sum formula works on its own.

But the GP trick still works. Multiply the entire sum by r, line it up shifted by one position, and subtract. The arithmetic part collapses its differences into a single constant d, turning the leftover into an ordinary GP.

<curious> And convergence comes for free when the size of r is below one. Both r to the n and n times r to the n die away, because geometric decay eventually overwhelms the linear growth of the AP label, so the infinite sum is finite.
The recognition skill is everything: spot an AGP by its shape — something linear in n, multiplied by r to the n minus one.

segments_hinglish.text: अब एक progression जो हमारे पहले से जाने दोनों को fuse करती है। एक arithmetico-geometric progression को एक GP समझो जिसके terms एक growing counter से लगातार re-weight हो रहे हैं।
board इसे concrete बना देता है। ऊपर एक AP लो, नीचे एक GP, और उन्हें term by term multiply करो — r to the k की geometric decay, AP के linear march से गुणा।
तो general term है a plus n minus one times d, all times r to the n minus one — AP factor और GP factor एक साथ multiply किए हुए।
यह सिर्फ़ एक abstraction नहीं है। finance में present-value और expected-value calculations — लगातार बढ़ते payments जिनमें हर एक fixed factor से discount हो — exactly AGP sums हैं।
यह रही summation की defining challenge: चूँकि हर term additive और multiplicative दोनों pattern रखता है, न AP sum formula अकेले काम करता है न GP sum formula।

पर GP trick फिर भी काम करता है। पूरे sum को r से multiply करो, एक position shift करके line up करो, और subtract करो। arithmetic part अपने differences को एक single constant d में collapse कर देता है, बचे हुए को एक ordinary GP में बदल देता है।

<curious> और convergence मुफ़्त में आती है जब r की size one से नीचे हो। r to the n और n times r to the n दोनों मर जाते हैं, क्योंकि geometric decay आख़िरकार AP label की linear growth को हरा देती है, तो infinite sum finite है।
recognition skill ही सब कुछ है: एक AGP को उसके shape से पहचानो — n में कुछ linear, r to the n minus one से गुणा।

57.title: Summing an AGP: multiply by r and subtract

board_content.text: The one technique that IS this subtopic
Subtract: every middle column leaves a clean $d\,r^k$.
Don't memorise the messy $S_n$ — re-derive with the subtraction every time.

segments_english.text: This one derivation is the entire subtopic, so let's walk it carefully. It is the GP sum trick applied one level up.
Write out the sum S sub n: a, plus a plus d times r, plus a plus two d times r squared, and so on to the last term.
Now multiply the whole line by r, which shifts every term one position to the right — the same move we used for the plain GP.
Subtract the second line from the first. The first column gives a bare a, and every middle column leaves a clean d times r to the k, because the AP differences collapse to the constant d.
Collecting everything, one minus r times S sub n equals a, plus d times the geometric sum r plus r squared up to r to the n minus one, minus the final leftover term.

That inner bracket is just a GP sum, so dividing through gives the full closed form: a over one minus r, plus d r times one minus r to the n minus one, over one minus r squared, minus the last-term correction.

Letting n go to infinity with the size of r below one kills both the r-to-the-n-minus-one and r-to-the-n pieces, leaving the compact sum to infinity: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared.
<whisper> One piece of exam wisdom: don't memorise that messy finite formula. Re-derive it with the multiply-by-r subtraction every single time — it is faster and far more error-proof under pressure.

segments_hinglish.text: यह एक derivation पूरा subtopic है, तो इसे ध्यान से चलते हैं। यह GP sum trick है, एक level ऊपर लगाया हुआ।
sum S sub n लिखो: a, plus a plus d times r, plus a plus two d times r squared, और ऐसे ही last term तक।
अब पूरी line को r से multiply करो, जो हर term को एक position दाएँ shift करता है — वही move जो हमने plain GP के लिए use किया था।
दूसरी line को पहली से subtract करो। पहला column एक bare a देता है, और हर middle column एक clean d times r to the k छोड़ता है, क्योंकि AP differences constant d में collapse हो जाते हैं।
सब इकट्ठा करने पर, one minus r times S sub n equals a, plus d times geometric sum r plus r squared से r to the n minus one तक, minus आख़िरी leftover term।
वो inner bracket बस एक GP sum है, तो divide करने पर पूरा closed form मिलता है: a over one minus r, plus d r times one minus r to the n minus one, over one minus r squared, minus last-term correction।

n को infinity तक ले जाने पर, r की size one से नीचे के साथ, r-to-the-n-minus-one और r-to-the-n दोनों pieces मर जाते हैं, बचता है compact sum to infinity: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared।
<whisper> एक exam wisdom: वो messy finite formula मत memorise करो। इसे हर बार multiply-by-r subtraction से re-derive करो — यह fast है और pressure में कहीं ज़्यादा error-proof।

58.title: The AGP formula set and its useful relatives

board_content.text: General term, both sums, and two must-know relatives
If $r = 1$ the AGP is just an AP — sum it with the AP formula, not this one.
These relatives also follow from differentiating the GP sum.

segments_english.text: Let's consolidate the AGP formulas, plus two relatives that show up constantly in Advanced problems.
The general term is a plus n minus one d, all times r to the n minus one — the AP factor times the GP factor.
The sum of n terms is the three-piece expression we just derived: a fixed term, a geometric middle term, and a last-term correction. Use it, but be ready to re-derive it if memory wobbles.
The sum to infinity is the clean one worth memorising: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared, valid only when the size of r is below one.
Now the two relatives. The sum of n times r to the n is r over one minus r squared — the workhorse for polynomial-times-geometric sums.
And the sum of n squared times r to the n is r times one plus r, over one minus r cubed. Together these two handle a huge range of Advanced series.
<whisper> Guard the r-equals-one case. When r is one the AGP degenerates into an ordinary AP, so sum it with the AP formula — never plug r equals one into these expressions and divide by zero.
One elegant footnote: both relatives also fall out of differentiating the geometric-series sum, if you prefer the calculus route.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो AGP formulas consolidate करें, साथ में दो relatives जो Advanced problems में लगातार आते हैं।
general term है a plus n minus one d, all times r to the n minus one — AP factor times GP factor।

n terms का sum वही three-piece expression है जो हमने अभी derive किया: एक fixed term, एक geometric middle term, और एक last-term correction। इसे use करो, पर memory डगमगाए तो re-derive करने को तैयार रहो।
sum to infinity वो clean है जो memorise करने लायक है: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared, valid सिर्फ़ तब जब r की size one से नीचे हो।
अब दो relatives। n times r to the n का sum है r over one minus r squared — polynomial-times-geometric sums का workhorse।
और n squared times r to the n का sum है r times one plus r, over one minus r cubed। ये दोनों मिलकर Advanced series की बड़ी range handle करते हैं।
<whisper> r-equals-one case को guard करो। जब r one हो तो AGP एक ordinary AP में बदल जाती है, तो इसे AP formula से sum करो — इन expressions में कभी r equals one डालकर zero से divide मत करो।
एक elegant footnote: दोनों relatives geometric-series sum को differentiate करने से भी निकलते हैं, अगर तुम्हें calculus route पसंद हो।

board_content.text: Sum to n terms: 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + … (x ≠ 1)
Here $a = 1$, $d = 1$, $r = x$. Use multiply-by-$x$.
The interior GP $1 + x + \dots + x^{n-1}$ is what survives the subtraction.

segments_english.text: Let's open the AGP examples with the archetype — the sum of one plus two x plus three x squared, and so on to n terms.
Read off the parameters. The arithmetic labels are one, two, three, so a is one and d is one; the geometric factor is x, so r is x. Now apply multiply-by-x.
Write the sum S sub n as one plus two x plus three x squared, up to n times x to the n minus one.
Multiply the whole line by x, shifting each term right: x plus two x squared, and so on to n times x to the n.

Subtracting, the coefficients collapse. What remains is a clean geometric series — one plus x up to x to the n minus one — minus the single leftover n times x to the n. That geometric part sums to one minus x to the n over one minus x.
Dividing through by one minus x gives the closed form: one minus x to the n over one minus x squared, minus n x to the n over one minus x.
<curious> Notice what did all the work — the interior geometric progression is exactly what survives the subtraction, and summing it is the whole game.

segments_hinglish.text: चलो AGP examples को archetype से खोलें — one plus two x plus three x squared का sum, और ऐसे ही n terms तक।
parameters पढ़ लो। arithmetic labels हैं one, two, three, तो a one है और d one; geometric factor x है, तो r x है। अब multiply-by-x apply करो।
sum S sub n को one plus two x plus three x squared लिखो, n times x to the n minus one तक।
पूरी line को x से multiply करो, हर term दाएँ shift करते हुए: x plus two x squared, और ऐसे ही n times x to the n तक।

subtract करने पर, coefficients collapse हो जाते हैं। जो बचता है वो एक clean geometric series है — one plus x से x to the n minus one तक — minus अकेला leftover n times x to the n। वो geometric part sum होकर one minus x to the n over one minus x बनता है।
one minus x से divide करने पर closed form मिलता है: one minus x to the n over one minus x squared, minus n x to the n over one minus x।
<curious> ध्यान दो किसने सारा काम किया — interior geometric progression exactly वही है जो subtraction में बचता है, और उसे sum करना ही पूरा खेल है।

60.title: Sum to infinity using the compact formula

board_content.text: Sum to infinity: 1 + 2/3 + 3/3² + 4/3³ + …
Check $|r| < 1$ first, then plug into the two-term $S_\infty$.

segments_english.text: Now the compact infinite-sum formula in action. We want the total of one plus two thirds plus three over three squared plus four over three cubed, forever.

Read off the parameters: the numerators one, two, three, four give a equals one and d equals one, and the denominators are powers of three, so r is one third. Crucially, its size is below one, so the sum exists.
Apply the two-term sum-to-infinity formula: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared.
The first piece is one over one minus one third, which is three halves.
The second piece is one third over one minus one third, squared — that is one third over four ninths, which simplifies to three quarters.
Adding them, three halves plus three quarters is nine quarters.

<curious> And the discipline stays the same as with any infinite GP — check the size of r is below one first, then simply plug into the two clean terms. No multiply-by-r grind needed once you trust the formula.

segments_hinglish.text: अब compact infinite-sum formula action में। हमें one plus two thirds plus three over three squared plus four over three cubed का total चाहिए, हमेशा के लिए।

parameters पढ़ो: numerators one, two, three, four देते हैं a equals one और d equals one, और denominators three की powers हैं, तो r one third है। crucially, इसकी size one से नीचे है, तो sum exist करता है।
two-term sum-to-infinity formula apply करो: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared।
पहला piece है one over one minus one third, यानी three halves।
दूसरा piece है one third over one minus one third, squared — यानी one third over four ninths, जो simplify होकर three quarters बनता है।
इन्हें add करने पर, three halves plus three quarters है nine quarters।
<curious> और discipline किसी भी infinite GP जैसा ही रहता है — पहले check करो कि r की size one से नीचे है, फिर बस दो clean terms में plug करो। formula पर भरोसा हो तो multiply-by-r की मेहनत नहीं चाहिए।

61.title: Reading off a and d from numerators

board_content.text: Sum to infinity: 3/1 + 5/2 + 7/4 + 9/8 + …
Numerators 3, 5, 7, 9 form an AP ($a = 3$, $d = 2$).
Denominators 1, 2, 4, 8 form a GP with $r = \tfrac12$.
Separate numerator (AP) from denominator (GP) to read $a$, $d$, $r$.

segments_english.text: This example rewards a clean first read — separating the arithmetic and geometric structure before touching the formula.
Look at the numerators three, five, seven, nine. They step up by two each time, so they are an AP with first term three and common difference two.
Now the denominators one, two, four, eight. They double each time, so they are a GP with ratio one half — and its size is safely below one.
So this is a genuine AGP with a equals three, d equals two, r equals one half. Apply the sum-to-infinity formula.
The first piece is three over one minus one half, which is six. The second is two times one half over one minus one half squared, which is one over one quarter, equal to four.
Adding, six plus four gives ten.
<curious> The key habit is that first split — read the numerator as the AP and the denominator as the GP, and the parameters a, d, and r fall out immediately, with no guesswork.

segments_hinglish.text: यह example एक clean पहली read का इनाम देता है — formula छूने से पहले arithmetic और geometric structure को अलग करना।
numerators three, five, seven, nine देखो। ये हर बार two से बढ़ते हैं, तो ये एक AP हैं first term three और common difference two के साथ।
अब denominators one, two, four, eight। ये हर बार double होते हैं, तो ये एक GP हैं ratio one half के साथ — और इसकी size सुरक्षित रूप से one से नीचे है।
तो यह एक genuine AGP है a equals three, d equals two, r equals one half के साथ। sum-to-infinity formula apply करो।
पहला piece है three over one minus one half, यानी six। दूसरा है two times one half over one minus one half squared, यानी one over one quarter, बराबर four।
add करने पर, six plus four देता है ten।
<curious> key habit वो पहला split है — numerator को AP की तरह पढ़ो और denominator को GP की तरह, और parameters a, d, और r तुरंत निकल आते हैं, बिना किसी guesswork के।

board_content.text: Sum to n terms: 1 + 3x + 5x² + 7x³ + … (x ≠ 1)
Coefficients 1, 3, 5, 7 give $a = 1$, $d = 2$; $r = x$.
The last coefficient is $a + (n-1)d = 1 + 2(n-1) = 2n-1$.
Same method, just $d = 2$ instead of $d = 1$.

segments_english.text: This Advanced example is the same machinery as before, but with a steeper arithmetic label to keep you honest about the constant d.
The coefficients are one, three, five, seven — odd numbers stepping by two — so a is one and d is two, while the geometric factor r is x.

Run the multiply-by-x subtraction. After lining up and subtracting, one minus x times S sub n equals one, plus two times the geometric block x plus x squared up to x to the n minus one, minus the last-term piece.
That geometric block sums to two x times one minus x to the n minus one, over one minus x, so we substitute it in.
Dividing by one minus x gives the closed form: one over one minus x, plus two x times one minus x to the n minus one over one minus x squared, minus two n minus one times x to the n over one minus x.

<whisper> Watch the last coefficient carefully. The final AP label is a plus n minus one times d, which is one plus two times n minus one, equal to two n minus one — not just n. Getting that wrong is the classic slip here.
So the method is identical to the archetype; the only change is carrying d equals two instead of d equals one throughout.

coefficients हैं one, three, five, seven — odd numbers two से बढ़ते हुए — तो a one है और d two है, जबकि geometric factor r x है।

multiply-by-x subtraction चलाओ। line up करके subtract करने के बाद, one minus x times S sub n equals one, plus two times geometric block x plus x squared से x to the n minus one तक, minus last-term piece।
वो geometric block sum होकर two x times one minus x to the n minus one, over one minus x बनता है, तो हम इसे substitute करते हैं।

one minus x से divide करने पर closed form मिलता है: one over one minus x, plus two x times one minus x to the n minus one over one minus x squared, minus two n minus one times x to the n over one minus x।
